svg.title: Shrinking the Hello timer versus enabling BFD, and the four tiers of a convergent response
svg.desc: Left panel compares two ways to detect failure faster. Shrinking Hello and dead timers reaches about one second and three seconds, costs CPU on every neighbour, has a high false-failover rate and is only for very simple environments. BFD reaches fifty to three hundred milliseconds, is very light because it has its own fast path, has a low false-failover rate, needs both ends configured, and is the production recommendation. Right panel shows four tiers of a convergent response by time scale: milliseconds for link detection, hundreds of milliseconds for local repair with fast reroute or backup paths, seconds for IGP SPF recomputation, and tens of seconds for BGP and policy recomputation. A warning strip names the common bad combination: one second Hello, three second dead timer, no SPF throttling, so every optic flap becomes a full SPF run.
svg.text: Detection is not convergence: they are measured in different units and paid for differently
The goal is recovery in the shortest time without letting one flap shake the whole area
1 s / 3 s, and below that the risk grows fast
every neighbour processes Hellos faster, for ever
BFD packets are tiny and run on their own fast path
high — a busy CPU simply misses Hellos
low — BFD has its own detection logic
both ends must support it and be paired correctly
TIERED RESPONSE — EACH TIER ABSORBS WHAT THE ONE ABOVE CANNOT
Happens only if tiers 1 and 2 fail.
The combination to refuse in a design review: Hello 1 s, dead 3 s, and no SPF throttle anywhere. An optic flap becomes
neighbour down → SPF run → neighbour up → SPF run, until the CPU is saturated and everything is slower than before.
Fast detection without flap suppression does not reduce the outage; it amplifies the noise that causes it.

Rest of the toolkit: incremental SPF where supported, partial route calculation which updates the table without rebuilding the tree, and LSA arrival suppression to cap how often a Type 1 can be regenerated.
